title: What is a fraction?
summary: Find out what a fraction like three quarters really means, with pizzas, pies, and chocolate bars.
objective: Name and write the fraction for a shape cut into equal pieces.

hook.prompt: Mia cuts a pizza into 4 pieces. One piece is huge and the other 3 are small. Mia takes the huge piece. Did she get a quarter of the pizza?

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 120 120' direction='ltr' class='w-40 h-40'><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='50' class='fill-muted stroke-foreground' stroke-width='2' /><path d='M60,60 L110,60 A50,50 0 0,1 10,60 Z' class='fill-amber-400 stroke-foreground' stroke-width='2' /><line x1='10' y1='60' x2='110' y2='60' class='stroke-foreground' stroke-width='2' /><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='35' y2='16.7' class='stroke-foreground' stroke-width='2' /><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='85' y2='16.7' class='stroke-foreground' stroke-width='2' /></svg>
visual.alt: A pizza cut into 4 pieces of different sizes: one shaded piece is the whole bottom half, and the top half is split into 3 small pieces.

options.text: Yes: she got 1 piece out of 4
options.feedback: She did get 1 of the 4 pieces. But look: her piece is half the pizza!

options.text: No: she got more than a quarter
No: she got less than a quarter
options.feedback: Look again: her piece is the biggest one. It's half the whole pizza.

hook.explanation: Mia's piece is half the pizza, which is more than a quarter. So why isn't 1 piece out of 4 a quarter here? Let's find out.

bricks.title: Fractions use equal pieces
bricks.body: A **fraction** is a part of a whole that is cut into **equal** pieces. Every piece must be the same size. Cut a chocolate bar into 2 equal pieces, and each piece is a **half**. Cut it into 3 equal pieces, and each one is a **third**. Cut it into 4 equal pieces, and each one is a **quarter**.

visual.html:
4 equal pieces: quarters ✓
4 pieces, not equal: not quarters ✗
visual.alt: Two chocolate bars, each in 4 pieces with one shaded: the first has 4 equal pieces, so each is a quarter; the second has one big piece and 3 small ones, so they are not quarters.

term.definition: A part of a whole that is cut into equal pieces.

bricks.prompt: Which bar is cut into thirds?

visual.alt: A bar cut into 3 equal pieces.
A bar cut into 3 pieces: one big piece and two small ones.

options.feedback: This bar has 3 pieces, but one is much bigger. Thirds must all be the same size.

visual.alt: A bar cut into 4 equal pieces.

options.feedback: These pieces are equal, but there are 4 of them. 4 equal pieces are quarters.

visual.alt: A bar cut into 2 equal pieces.

options.feedback: These pieces are equal, but there are only 2. 2 equal pieces are halves.

bricks.hint: Look for 3 pieces that are all the same size.
bricks.explanation: Thirds means 3 pieces that are all the same size. Only this bar has 3 equal pieces.

bricks.title: Writing a fraction
bricks.body: We write a fraction as two numbers with a line between them. One piece of a bar cut into 4 equal pieces is \( \tfrac{1}{4} \). We say "one quarter". The **bottom number** tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into: 4. The **top number** tells how many of those pieces we mean: 1.

visual.html:
14
pieces we meanequal pieces in all
visual.alt: A bar cut into 4 equal pieces with 1 shaded, next to the fraction 1 over 4: the 1 is labelled pieces we mean, and the 4 is labelled equal pieces in all.

term.definition: The bottom number of a fraction: how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.

bricks.prompt: Ben says this bar shows \( \tfrac{1}{3} \) shaded, because 1 piece is shaded and 3 are not. What fraction is really shaded?

visual.alt: A bar cut into 4 equal pieces, with 1 piece shaded.

options.feedback: That's Ben's mistake. The bottom number counts all the equal pieces, shaded or not.
3 pieces are not shaded. The top number counts the pieces we mean: the shaded one.
The numbers are upside down. The pieces in all go on the bottom.

bricks.hint: Count every piece in the bar, shaded or not.
bricks.explanation:
The bar has 4 equal pieces in all, so the bottom number is 4.
1 piece is shaded, so the top number is 1.

bricks.prompt: Each piece of a chocolate bar is \( \tfrac{1}{5} \) of the bar. How many equal pieces is the bar cut into?

options.feedback: 1 is the top number: it means one piece. The bottom number tells how many pieces in all.
Don't add the two numbers. The bottom number alone tells how many pieces in all.
4 is how many are left after you take one. The whole bar starts with 5.

bricks.hint: Which number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into?
bricks.explanation: The bottom number of \( \tfrac{1}{5} \) is 5, so the whole bar is cut into 5 equal pieces.

bricks.title: The top number counts your pieces
bricks.body: The top number can be more than 1. A pizza has 8 equal slices, and you eat 3. You ate \( \tfrac{3}{8} \) of the pizza. The slices left over make a fraction too. There are 5 slices left, so \( \tfrac{5}{8} \) of the pizza is left. The bottom number stays 8, because the whole pizza had 8 slices.

visual.html: 3 slices eaten5 slices left
visual.alt: A pizza cut into 8 equal slices: 3 shaded slices are eaten and 5 plain slices are left.

term.definition: The top number of a fraction: how many of the equal pieces we mean.

bricks.prompt: Leo's pizza has 8 equal slices. He eats 3 of them. Build the fraction of the pizza that Leo ate.

mistakes.feedback: 5 is the slices left over. The top number counts the slices Leo ate.
8 is all the slices in the pizza. That number goes on the bottom.
3 is the slices Leo ate. That number goes on top.
Don't add the numbers. The bottom number is all the slices in the pizza.

bricks.hint: Top: the slices Leo ate. Bottom: all the slices in the pizza.
bricks.explanation:
Leo ate 3 slices, so the top number is 3.
The pizza had 8 equal slices, so the bottom number is 8.
Leo ate \( \tfrac{3}{8} \).

bricks.prompt: Grandma cuts a pie into 6 equal slices. The family eats 4 of them. What fraction of the pie is left?

options.feedback: That's the part the family ate. Count the slices that are left instead.
The bottom number counts all the slices in the whole pie, not just the ones eaten.
The numbers are upside down. All the slices in the pie go on the bottom.

bricks.hint: First count the slices left. Then count all the slices in the whole pie.
bricks.explanation:
6 − 4 = 2 slices are left: that's the top number.
The pie had 6 equal slices: that's the bottom number.
So \( \tfrac{2}{6} \) is left.

visual.alt: A square cut into 4 equal squares, with 3 of them shaded.
A square cut into 4 pieces of different sizes: one big plain half, and 3 small shaded pieces in the other half.

options.feedback: 3 of the 4 pieces are shaded, but the pieces aren't the same size. They aren't quarters, so this isn't three quarters.

visual.alt: A square cut into 4 equal squares, with 1 of them shaded.

options.feedback: Only 1 of the 4 equal pieces is shaded. That's \( \tfrac{1}{4} \). The top number says 3 pieces should be shaded.

visual.alt: A bar cut into 7 equal pieces, with 3 of them shaded.

options.feedback: 3 pieces are shaded, but there are 7 pieces in all. That's \( \tfrac{3}{7} \). The bottom number counts every piece.

challenge.hint: Check three things: are the pieces equal, are there 4 in all, and are 3 shaded?
challenge.explanation:
This square has 4 equal pieces, so the bottom number is 4.
3 of them are shaded, so the top number is 3.

takeaways: A fraction is a part of a whole that is cut into equal pieces.
The bottom number counts all the equal pieces in the whole.
The top number counts the pieces you mean, like the slices you ate or the slices left.
